messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Samir stood in the kitchen of his forty-year-old self, listening to the water main click on, and felt the familiar press of that October night returning to his skin. The retaining wall behind his neighborhood had given way, and the rushing floodwater had torn through his front door just as he stepped toward the garage. He was certain he had misjudged the slope, moving into the current at the exact second the drywall shuddered and pinned him. Now, when the memory surfaces, it does not arrive as a simple recollection; the roar of the water, the chill of the mud on his arms, and the heavy pressure of his wife’s hand on his back return all at once, making the past feel completely real across all his senses. He looks back at his life before the disaster and recognizes a man who used to be happy, who laughed easily at dinner parties and planned summer trips without hesitation. He had come to believe that nothing good could happen to him anymore, and though he forces himself to think only positive thoughts, the repetition feels like a manual exercise. He sits with this quiet certainty that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, that he had placed himself in the wrong room at the wrong hour. Over the following months, Samir found his body braced for another collapse, and the symptoms settled into his days without demanding each other. An unexpected movement nearby, even the simple glide of a colleague’s rolling chair, would make him react as if the floor were giving way beneath him. He began identifying escape routes before he felt comfortable anywhere, pacing the perimeter of restaurants and noting emergency exits before his wife could sit down. When she touched his shoulder from behind, he would startle with quiet alarm, his breath catching as though the water were already rising again. The memories of that night arrived out of order; sometimes he would first recall the sound of his front door tearing off its hinges, only to remember the shudder of the floorboards hours later. Yet the clarity remained, especially the auditory layer. In the stillness of his home office, he would hear the specific crack of the water main, sharp and metallic, echoing in his head even when the room was completely quiet. His work as a software engineer provided a structured environment, yet it was not immune to the strain. During daily stand-up meetings in the glass-walled conference room, he kept his eyes on the glass doors, calculating the distance to the hallway if the fire alarm sounded. A dropped tablet or a sudden gesture from a developer would trigger the same defensive tensing he had learned at home. At work, he also avoided medical cues, steering clear of hospitals and dreading physical examinations where the bright lights and the rustle of paper gowns felt like unnecessary threats. Beneath that surface of routine, he ruminated about how to get even with the site foreman whose earlier warnings about the soil had been ignored, replaying the conversation until the man’s voice felt like a personal failure. He was not avoiding them because one symptom drove another; they simply coexisted in his days. His marriage remained steady, though he noticed his wife waiting for a smile that sometimes took longer to arrive, and he returned her gaze with a quiet acknowledgment rather than the easy warmth he used to offer. What finally brought Samir to seek help was a quiet Tuesday when he stood in his kitchen and realized he could not remember the last time he had slept through the night without bracing for a sound. He did not want to dismantle his routines, but he hoped someone might help him untangle the memories, so the past would stop feeling like it was happening in the present. He told his therapist that he was not afraid of the water or the falling debris, but of the suddenness, of being caught off guard, of carrying the weight of a situation that others had navigated more easily. He was ready, he said, to stop forcing the positive thoughts and to let the sequence of events settle into the order they actually happened.
